$comment: SHARED CONTRACT — the CONFIG RESOLVE REPORT seam ([F9], 2026-07-30).
The question the product could not answer: 「내 config가 먹었는가」. The admin surface
had exactly one config route, POST /admin/reload-configs, which refreshes caches, fans a
reload event out to every worker, and returns NOTHING about what any of it did. Ten config
files, one write-only button.
WHAT THIS FILE PINS, AND WHY IT IS A SEAM AND NOT A UNIT TEST
The server sorts declarations into three named populations and NAMES THE REASON. The
client renders the server's string. Those are two implementations of one agreement, and
the failure mode is not a crash — it is the client quietly growing its own opinion about
what counts as ineffective. That is the hardcoded-copy class U6 deleted six instances of,
and it passes every server test ever written. Only a seam contract catches it.
server -> contracts/config_resolve_report/test_report_contract.py
(reachable from the default suite via server/tests/test_config_resolve_report_contract.py)
client -> node contracts/config_resolve_report/client_harness.mjs
THE VOCABULARY IS CLOSED AND BORROWED, NOT INVENTED
All four words already exist in the runtime degradation vocabulary (main.CHIP_TRACE_*).
This round moves the same distinctions one layer up — from 'what did this request find'
to 'what did this config declare' — so a second vocabulary would be a second dialect for
the same idea. `reasons` below is the whole list. A fifth word is a contract change.
WHAT THE CLIENT MAY AND MAY NOT DO
MAY  : switch on population (effective/ineffective/rejected) — that is structure, and the
server decided it. Render `detail`. Render `fields.*` as literal table cells.
MAY  : read `vocabulary.reasons` from the response for filters/labels-by-key.
MUST NOT: contain the reason words as literals, or carry its own Korean explanation for
any of them. The moment it does, the two sides can disagree about a rule's state
and the server's answer stops being the answer. `forbidden_client_literals` is
what the node harness greps for, and it is the whole point of this file.

reason_meanings.$comment: Prose for humans. The machine check is that server REASONS == vocabulary.reasons.
reason_meanings.not_declared: a declaration required for the effect is absent (knob off, or zero candidate_for)
reason_meanings.mapping_unavailable: the declaration failed to parse/validate and is not in effect
reason_meanings.scope_unresolved: the declaration parses and acts, but its scope does not pin the decision key
reason_meanings.not_reached: an enclosing switch is off, so this declaration is never consulted

envelope.$comment: Required keys at each level. Extra keys are allowed (additive change stays cheap).

invariants.name: every ineffective and rejected entry names a reason
invariants.why: An entry that says 'no effect' without saying why sends the operator back to the daemon log, which is the state this round exists to end.

invariants.name: every effective entry has reason == null
invariants.why: A reason on an effective entry means the two populations are not actually distinguishing anything.

invariants.name: every reason and every warning comes from vocabulary.reasons
invariants.why: The client cannot render a word it has never been told about, and a free-form reason is how a closed vocabulary dies.

invariants.name: every entry carries a non-empty detail string
invariants.why: detail IS the client's rendering. An empty one forces the client to compose its own sentence, which is exactly the derivation this contract forbids.

invariants.name: counts equal the population lengths
invariants.why: A badge computed from a count that disagrees with the list is the cheapest possible lie.

invariants.name: a missing config file is `exists: false`, never a rejection
invariants.why: Same rule as /graph/mapping-summary. Conflating them makes the rejection list non-empty in a healthy system, and a list that cries wolf gets ignored.

invariants.name: the client contains none of forbidden_client_literals
invariants.why: The U6 class. A client that knows the words can decide for itself what they mean.

$comment: Grepped by client_harness.mjs across client2/src. These are SERVER words: the client
receives them inside data and must never contain them as source literals.
`vocabulary.reasons` arrives in the response, so a client CAN iterate it — that is the
point. Writing one of them down is what turns a rendered fact into a client opinion.
MEASURED, not imagined. The live enrichment_rules.json declares two rules and five
reference views, and NOT ONE view declares `candidate_for`. So a `auto_confirm: true`
here would read as ON and do nothing. This case is the reason F9 exists; it is written
as a vector so that the day someone declares a candidate column, this expectation
changes DELIBERATELY rather than silently.

cases.$comment: The narrow view declares its candidate column. This is what 'it worked' looks like.

$comment: THE TRAP, measured on the live config. `같은 lot 전체 슬롯` keys on lot alone. Declaring
candidate_for on it yields `single` — NOT `ambiguous` — because wafer_slot_history holds
one row for that lot, and that one wafer_id is then written onto 23 different slots.
So the danger is not visible from the refusal vocabulary at runtime: the runtime says
`single` and is not lying. It is only visible from the DECLARATION — the view binds a
strict subset of the decision key — which is why it has to be surfaced HERE, before
anyone turns the knob on, and not in the sweep afterwards.

cases.$comment: Same reason class, different `detail`. The client renders the sentence, so the two stay distinguishable without the client knowing why.
`"true"` is the spelling an operator reaches for. Today it warns once into a log and falls back to OFF.
The per-rule declaration is correct and complete; it is simply never consulted. `not_declared` would be a lie about the rule.
The declaration parses as JSON and is still wrong: `lot` is a decision key, not a target. `valid_die_ref`-style shape drift, one layer down.

.sample does. The global switch therefore defaults to true and nobody knows it. This
is precisely the 'where did this value come from' question the settings list answers,

settings_cases.$comment: The in-effect value is the default AND the bad declaration appears in `rejected`. Both halves are needed: one says what is running, the other says what was ignored.
